title: The Chan monastery
hookLine: Mazu and Baizhang: work, meals and meditation shaped into one life

cards: A wooden board is struck outside the meditation hall, and the monks file out. Not to chant this time. To the fields, with hoes and baskets.

The cook is already at the stove, the youngest monks are hauling water, and somewhere among them, bent over a row of vegetables, is the abbot. In a Chan monastery, the stories say, nobody was too senior to dig.
Two teachers stand behind this picture: Mazu, who shook his students awake, and his student Baizhang, who gave the community its shape.

teach.h: MAZU: THIS VERY MIND IS BUDDHA.
teach.b: First, Mazu. He was a teacher in Huineng's line, remembered for blunt answers, shouts and sudden questions. In the Gateless Gate, a monk asks him what Buddha is, and Mazu answers: this very mind is Buddha.
Not somewhere else, not later. This mind, the one asking. Second, Baizhang and the rules.
Chan is remembered as a school of meditation, and you might expect a Chan monastery to do nothing but sit.

teach.h: BAIZHANG: RULES FOR A WHOLE DAY.
teach.b: Tradition credits Baizhang with shaping rules for Chan communities, and those rules put sitting inside a whole day: a hall for meditation, meals eaten together in order and in quiet, and shared work for everyone.

teach.h: WORK, MEALS AND SITTING AS ONE LIFE.
teach.b: Third, work, meals and sitting as one life. In that picture, digging the garden isn't time off from practice, and washing the bowls isn't a chore to rush through.
The same attention that watches the breath in the hall watches the hoe in the soil. Fourth, water and firewood. A layman named Pang, who studied with Mazu, put it in a short verse.
His supernatural powers and marvelous deeds, he said, were these: carrying water and hauling firewood.

It's a joke, and it isn't. If this very mind is Buddha, as Mazu said, then it's this mind that carries the water. A modern day has its own version of Baizhang's fields: dishes, laundry, commuting, typing.
The Chan monastery's claim is that none of it has to be wasted time.

how: In Chan and Zen monasteries today, residents share daily work periods, often called samu in Japanese, alongside meditation and meals eaten together in a set form.

games.why: tradition credits Baizhang with rules that made shared work part of the day, alongside sitting and meals. the abbot went to the fields too.

practice: Choose a chore you'll do today, dishes, folding clothes, sweeping, and walk through it slowly in your mind: the water's temperature, the weight of the cloth, the sound of the broom.
Notice where the mind usually runs off to while you do it. Then come back to the breath, and let the chore wait for its moment.
